title: Quasi-Experimental Designs: When Random Assignment Is Impossible
description: Navigate nonequivalent control groups, interrupted time-series designs, regression discontinuity, and selection confounds.

slides.title: The Compromise with Reality 🏙️
slides.content:
# When You Cannot Randomly Assign

In many applied psychological, clinical, and policy domains, random assignment is ethically impossible or practically unfeasible:

* You cannot randomly assign pregnant mothers to smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol.
* You cannot randomly assign employees to experience a company bankruptcy.
* You cannot randomly assign children to attend School A vs. School B.

A **quasi-experimental design** resembles a true experiment by comparing different conditions or interventions, but **lacks random assignment** of participants to those conditions. Because participants arrive with pre-existing differences, the primary threat is **Selection Bias**.

quizData.question: What is the defining distinction between a true experiment and a quasi-experiment?

options.text: True experiments have independent variables; quasi-experiments never have independent variables
True experiments use random assignment to conditions; quasi-experiments lack random assignment
Quasi-experiments are only conducted on animals
True experiments are not subject to ethical IRB review

quizData.explanation: Quasi-experiments evaluate treatments across groups or over time, but participants cannot be randomly assigned, creating selection threats to internal validity.

slides.title: Two Classic Quasi-Experimental Designs 📊
slides.content:
## Standard Methodological Solutions

| Design | Architecture & Procedures | Strengths & Vulnerabilities |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Nonequivalent Control Group Pretest-Posttest Design** | Compares an intact, pre-existing treatment group (e.g., Classroom 1) to an intact comparison group (Classroom 2) before and after intervention. | Administering a pretest establishes whether groups were equivalent at baseline; vulnerable to **Selection-History** and **Selection-Maturation** interactions. |
| **Interrupted Time-Series Design** | Takes multiple repeated measurements of the dependent variable before and after an abrupt policy change or intervention event. (e.g., O1, O2, O3, O4 -> Intervention -> O5, O6, O7, O8). | Demonstrates pre-intervention secular trends and post-intervention discontinuity; rules out simple maturation, but vulnerable to simultaneous historical events. |

For example, psychologists used an interrupted time series to study whether a state mandatory seatbelt law reduced traffic fatalities by tracking monthly road fatalities for 36 months before and after the law took effect.

quizData.question: A hospital tracks nurse absenteeism rates every month for 12 months, implements a workplace wellness program in Month 13, and tracks absenteeism for another 12 months. What quasi-experimental design is this?

options.text: True laboratory experiment with double blinding

quizData.explanation: Taking multiple longitudinal measurements before and after a specific discrete intervention event is the definition of an interrupted time-series design.

slides.title: Psychology Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
### The Power of Multiple Pretests

Why take multiple measurements before the intervention in a time-series? Because a single pretest cannot show you if the variable was already naturally improving or declining! Multiple pretests establish the baseline slope and seasonal fluctuations, allowing you to prove true post-intervention discontinuity.
